items.answer: A prototype is a lightweight implementation, with much lower requirements for resources, skilled manpower, and cost than a full implementation, that can be built quickly to model or demonstrate a design idea and to test whether it will work in practice. It can be discarded after testing or refined into the final product.

Horizontal prototype is a prototype that depicts the entire interface at a surface level, showing its look, feel, and appearance without functionality or interaction, so it is used to discuss, brainstorm, and elicit feedback about whether the interface is understandable, intuitive, and usable.

A vertical prototype is a type of prototype that implements a few selected features likely to be most commonly used in depth, from the first screen to the last, to represent interactions rather than all system functionalities.

A low-fidelity prototype is a prototype of an interface made without technological intervention, programming, code, or a computer, using non-digital materials such as paper, cardboard, or wood, and to represent interaction it needs a series of interface sketches, often called a storyboard, rather than a single sketch.

A storyboard is a low-fidelity prototype consisting of a series of interface sketches, each a keyframe, that captures the sequence of user actions and screen changes for a specific task from beginning to end.

Interactive system is a system in which interaction takes place between the computer or system and the user, a lay person who is not necessarily a technology expert and who wants to use the system rather than understand how it works.

questions.question: What is a throwaway prototype?
options: A prototype made for expert evaluation and then retained
A prototype made from tested modules and then integrated
A prototype made for quick evaluation and then discarded
A prototype made as a simple whole system and then refined
questions.explanation: A throwaway prototype is used for quick evaluation and is discarded afterward, rather than retained, integrated from modules, or refined into a larger system.

questions.question: Why should a throwaway prototype be easy and fast to create?
options: Because slow creation makes working with it expensive
Because slow creation makes refining the whole system expensive
Because slow creation makes testing the final product expensive
Because slow creation makes integrating modules expensive
questions.explanation: If a throwaway prototype is not easy and fast to create, working with it becomes expensive; the other costs are tied to incremental or evolutionary prototyping, not to the throwaway purpose.

questions.question: How does an evolutionary prototype differ from an incremental prototype?
options: It builds separate modules, tests them, and then integrates them
It refines one whole-system prototype until it becomes the final product
It uses one module to replace the rest of the system
It makes a low-fidelity sketch for quick evaluation and then discards it
questions.explanation: Evolutionary prototyping starts with a simpler version of the whole system and refines it into the final product, while incremental prototyping builds and tests modules separately before integration.

data.text: Prototyping in system implementation takes three different forms. Throwaway prototypes give cheap, disposable evaluation, while incremental prototypes build the system module by module. Evolutionary prototypes instead refine a whole-system version from a simple start until it becomes the final product.
points: In system implementation, prototypes can be used as throwaway, incremental, or evolutionary prototypes.
Throwaway prototypes are used for quick evaluation, mainly with easy low-fidelity mockups, and then discarded.
Incremental prototypes are created when the design divides the system into modules, each separately prototyped, tested, and integrated.
Evolutionary prototypes begin simple, then are tested, refined, and expanded into a final whole system, not modules.

questions.question: What makes expert evaluation different from robust evaluation?
options: It can be a low-cost, early design-stage review
It can be a long-duration, full-setup design-stage review
It can be a user-heavy, full-setup design-stage review
It can be a resource-heavy, full-setup design-stage review
questions.explanation: Expert evaluation is a low-cost way to check a design in the early stage, whereas robust evaluation typically needs more resources and a fuller setup.

questions.question: What can be enough to start a quick expert evaluation?
options: A final product and a programmer team
A storyboard and a client team
A high-fidelity prototype and an end-user team
A low-fidelity prototype and an evaluator team
questions.explanation: The minimum prerequisites are at least a low-fidelity prototype and a team of evaluators. Higher-quality prototypes are better, but they are not required to begin.

questions.question: Who should mainly serve as the evaluators in a quick expert evaluation?
options: Design-team members or problem-domain designers as evaluators
External usability consultants with no design role as evaluators
End users chosen from the target audience as evaluators
Project stakeholders who will buy the system as evaluators
questions.explanation: Quick expert evaluation is a usability test whose team is primarily the design team or skilled designers with problem-domain knowledge. End users may be included only optionally, because these evaluators are assumed to give user-like feedback.

questions.question: What does each evaluator do during a quick expert evaluation?
options: Observe end users with the prototype and note the issues those users report
Evaluate the prototype independently and report the usability issues they perceive
Discuss the prototype with the other evaluators and record their joint findings
Vote for the most serious usability issues and record the shared findings
questions.explanation: Each evaluator works independently on the prototype and produces a personal report of perceived usability issues. The design team or team lead then combines those reports into a final list.

data.text: Expert evaluation is a fast, low-cost way to check a prototype early in design, requiring at least a low-fidelity prototype and an evaluator team. It differs from full usability testing because the team is usually designers or domain experts, sometimes with a few end users, since their feedback is quicker and cheaper to obtain. With three to five evaluators, each independently reports perceived usability issues, and the design team or lead combines those reports into a final issue list.
points: Expert evaluation is a quick, cheap early-stage prototype evaluation, unlike robust evaluation.
Expert evaluation needs at least a low-fidelity prototype, ideally higher-quality, and an evaluator team.
Although a usability test, expert evaluation mainly uses design-team or domain experts, optionally a few end users.
Experts can replace end users because they are assumed user-like, quicker, and cheaper to engage.
Three to five evaluators are sufficient, and each independently reports usability issues, which the lead combines.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of a cognitive walkthrough?
options: To record user satisfaction after public release
To inspect a prototype for usability problems
To validate a finished product with end users
To test implementation code for performance faults
questions.explanation: A cognitive walkthrough is a usability inspection method in which evaluators examine a prototype to uncover usability problems. It is not a full product validation, code performance test, or post-release satisfaction survey.

questions.question: What is the minimum prototype requirement for a cognitive walkthrough?
options: A high-fidelity vertical prototype that lowers the cost of evaluation
A medium-fidelity horizontal prototype that shows many screens
A throwaway vertical prototype that demonstrates one task
A low-fidelity vertical prototype that supports several tasks
questions.explanation: A cognitive walkthrough needs at least a low-fidelity vertical prototype that can support several tasks. Higher fidelity can be used but is not the minimum, and a prototype limited to one task does not meet the requirement.

questions.question: How do evaluators use a task scenario in a cognitive walkthrough?
options: They rate how realistic the task description sounds
They compare the task with a general usability checklist
They select the screens they expect the user to visit
They perform the interface-level actions for the task
questions.explanation: The task scenario is converted into interface-level actions, and evaluators perform those actions with the prototype. Merely predicting screens, judging realism, or checking a general list does not capture the task-based evaluation.

questions.question: What do usability questions guide evaluators to do in a cognitive walkthrough?
options: To report where and why they found difficulty
To justify a simple affirm-or-deny verdict
To choose the evaluator whose findings seem most serious
To confirm that the interface looks aesthetically pleasing
questions.explanation: Usability questions serve as guidelines for identifying likely user problems, and each should lead to a detailed explanation of where and why the interface caused difficulty. A simple yes-or-no verdict, aesthetic judgment, or ranking of evaluators does not serve that purpose.

data.text: A cognitive walkthrough is an expert inspection in which a small team uses a prototype to anticipate usability problems. The evaluators work from a task scenario converted into interface-level actions and apply pre-framed usability questions as guidelines. They produce detailed reports explaining where and why the interface or interaction is difficult, and those reports are combined and analyzed to identify broader usability issues.
points: A cognitive walkthrough is a quick expert evaluation method that inspects a prototype to find usability problems.
It needs a vertical prototype, at least low-fidelity, such as storyboards, and three to five evaluators.
Evaluators follow a task scenario converted into interface-level tasks and perform those actions in the prototype.
Evaluators answer pre-framed usability questions with detailed reports explaining where and why the interface or interaction is difficult.
The evaluators' reports are collected, combined, and analyzed at the end to identify broader usability issues.

questions.question: Which description fits heuristic evaluation?
options: A scenario-driven inspection of the whole system
A checklist-based review of the whole system
A performance-measuring trial of the whole system
A task-based observation of the whole system
questions.explanation: Heuristic evaluation assesses a prototype by checking heuristics across the system rather than by observing users complete tasks or scenarios. Task-based observation and scenario-driven inspection belong to other usability methods.

questions.question: In prototype terms, how does heuristic evaluation differ from cognitive walkthrough?
options: It mainly uses detailed prototypes, with sketch prototypes optional
It mainly uses task-driven prototypes, with whole-system prototypes optional
It mainly uses horizontal prototypes, with vertical prototypes optional
It mainly uses vertical prototypes, with horizontal prototypes optional
questions.explanation: Heuristic evaluation can be done early on simple, primarily horizontal prototypes, while cognitive walkthrough requires a vertical prototype that supports the tasks being walked through.

questions.question: Why do broader usability checklists usually contain fewer heuristics than detailed system-specific checklists?
options: They cover general principles instead of one particular interface
They cover resource use instead of one particular interface
They cover task performance instead of one particular interface
They cover final products instead of one particular interface
questions.explanation: A broader checklist is less specific to any particular interface, so it includes fewer, more general usability principles rather than detailed interface-specific items.

questions.question: What scope does Nielsen's usability set have?
options: A resource-based checklist for most interactive systems
A detailed checklist for one particular class of systems
A task-based checklist for most interactive systems
A general checklist for most interactive systems
questions.explanation: Nielsen's set is a general usability checklist that, although rooted in graphical user interfaces, applies to most interactive systems. It is not a task-based or resource-based checklist for one class of systems.

data.text: Heuristic evaluation is an expert-based way to review a prototype comprehensively by comparing it against usability checklists. Nielsen's 10 heuristics provide a general, 1994 checklist that can be used early on low-fidelity prototypes, especially horizontal ones. In practice, a small team of evaluators independently checks each heuristic, explains violations, and combines their reports to reveal the major usability issues.
points: Heuristic evaluation checks a whole prototype without tasks, using system-specific or broader, shorter heuristics checklists.
Nielsen's 10 heuristics are a general 1994 interactive set: status, match, control, consistency, error prevention, recognition, flexibility, minimalism, recovery, help.
Nielsen's heuristics can spot problems early on low-fidelity prototypes, mainly horizontal, with vertical optional, unlike cognitive walkthrough.
Heuristic evaluation uses at least three to five evaluators, who may be design-team or expert designers.
Each evaluator reports heuristic violations with reasons, and combined reports identify major usability issues.

activities.title: Order the steps of heuristic evaluation

items.title: Order the steps of heuristic evaluation
steps: The prototype and checklist are given to evaluators
The prototype is checked against each heuristic
Heuristic violations are reported with reasons
The reports are combined into a final issue list

options: Throwaway prototype
Paper prototype
Evolutionary prototype
Incremental prototype
items.reason: Throwaway, incremental, and evolutionary prototypes are ways a prototype can be used, while a paper prototype is a low-fidelity prototype for a cognitive walkthrough.

options: Check each heuristic
User control and freedom
Consistency and standards
Visibility of system status
items.reason: Visibility of system status, user control and freedom, and consistency and standards are Nielsen heuristics, whereas checking each heuristic is the action performed in heuristic evaluation.

options: Perform the actions
Create a scenario
Tick the checklist
Convert the task
items.reason: Creating a scenario, converting the task into interface-level tasks, and performing those actions are cognitive-walkthrough steps, while ticking a checklist is the evaluator's task in heuristic evaluation.

questions.question: Why are low-fidelity cardboard mockups and paper sketches particularly suitable for throwaway prototypes?
questions.reference_answer: Throwaway prototypes are made for quick evaluation and then discarded. Low-fidelity cardboard mockups and paper sketches are suitable because they are less costly, so discarding them does not incur significant cost. Throwaway prototypes should be easy and fast to create, because otherwise working with them becomes expensive.

questions.question: How do incremental and evolutionary prototypes differ in the way a system is built from prototypes?
questions.reference_answer: Incremental prototyping is used when system design divides the system into units or modules; each module is separately prototyped and tested, then integrated. Evolutionary prototyping instead builds the whole system from the beginning. It starts with a simpler version, refines it, adds more functionalities, and alters it based on testing until it becomes the final product.

questions.question: Why can expert evaluation be carried out mainly by design-team members or domain experts, even though usability testing primarily involves users?
questions.reference_answer: Design-team members or domain experts are assumed to have user-like experience in the problem domain, so their feedback likely reflects users. Engaging them is less complicated, quicker, and cheaper than engaging a full evaluation team with end users.

questions.question: Why does a cognitive walkthrough need a vertical prototype, while heuristic evaluation can mainly use a horizontal low-fidelity prototype?
questions.reference_answer: Cognitive walkthrough requires a vertical prototype because its low-fidelity prototype must support several tasks, and evaluators then perform the interface-level actions from a scenario. Heuristic evaluation has no task scenario or task performance; evaluators only check a heuristic checklist. Therefore it can be based on simple low-fidelity, primarily horizontal prototypes, with vertical prototypes optional.
